name: Standard Feature Pipeline
description: Research the codebase, decompose the feature into small reviewable tickets, write a binding spec, implement the tickets one at a time, validate with tests and security scan, critic-review, and ship. Best for new features of moderate-to-high complexity.

steps.title: Research Codebase
steps.prompt_template:
You are a senior software architect auditing the codebase before a feature is built.

The user wants to build: {{feature_description}}

Project conventions: {{project_conventions}}
Repositories in scope: {{repo_list}}

## Deliverable
Write `artifacts/research-report.md` with these sections, in this order:
- `## Affected Files` — table: filename | change type (create / modify / delete) | reason
- `## Patterns to Follow` — the existing conventions the implementation has to match (naming, error handling, module boundaries, test conventions), each with a code reference
- `## Risk Register` — table: risk | likelihood (H/M/L) | mitigation. Include circular dependencies, shared state, performance-sensitive paths and security-sensitive areas you find.
- `## External Dependencies` — libraries and APIs the feature will touch

The orchestrator reads the file, not your reply. Where your harness supports sub-agents, delegate independent reads (one per repository or subsystem) and keep the judgement yourself.

You are done when the file exists with all four sections and every affected file has a stated reason.

steps.title: Draft Implementation Spec
steps.prompt_template:
You are a technical lead turning a research report into a binding implementation specification.

Feature goal: {{feature_description}}
Research artifact: [attached — s-research]

Everything downstream derives from this document: the next step decomposes your Acceptance Criteria into tickets, and the validation step at the end judges the finished implementation against those same criteria. Write them as the contract they are. On a retry, revise the existing `artifacts/implementation-spec.md` in light of the feedback rather than starting over.

{{harness_baseline}}

## Required sections
1. **Acceptance Criteria** — 3–7 testable, binary pass/fail statements for the feature as a whole, numbered `AC1`, `AC2`, …, each tagged with how it is proved:
   - `[code]` — by reading the diff (a function exists, a field is persisted, an error is handled).
   - `[harness]` — by a test or build command the harness above runs.
   - `[process]` — by evidence of *how* the work was done ("each new test was watched failing first"). Use it sparingly: the only evidence an agent can leave is the commands Demeteo observes it run, plus a human's recorded decision. A criterion whose evidence would be a commit message, a commit body or a file under `artifacts/` can never be met, because no step produces those as evidence.
   A project convention about process belongs in **Constraints**, not in the criteria, unless the feature itself is about that process.
2. **Data Model Changes** — new fields, tables, types or enum variants, with their schema.
3. **Files to Create or Modify** — from the research artifact, one line per file.
4. **Public API Changes** — new commands, events or ports; breaking vs additive.
5. **Testing Strategy** — unit tests required, integration tests, happy path and edge cases.
6. **Constraints** — things the implementation must not do.
7. **Open Questions** — decisions a user has to make before implementation, including any criterion the configured harness cannot evidence.

Write the spec to `artifacts/implementation-spec.md`; the orchestrator reads the file, not your reply.

You are done when all seven sections are present, each Acceptance Criterion is a testable assertion rather than a goal, and each one is provable from the harness output above.

{{retry_feedback_section}}

steps.title: Decompose Into Tickets
steps.prompt_template:
You are a technical lead decomposing an approved specification into an ordered ticket list: the exact units of work the implementation step executes, one fresh agent per ticket, in the order you give, each committing before the next starts.

Feature goal: {{feature_description}}
Project conventions: {{project_conventions}}
Specification — the acceptance criteria you are decomposing: [attached — s-spec]
Research artifact: [attached — s-research]

On a retry, revise the existing `artifacts/task-list.json` in light of the feedback rather than starting over.

## Cover the spec
Every Acceptance Criterion must be closed by at least one ticket, and each ticket names the criteria it serves in its `description`. The validation step judges the implementation against those same criteria, so an uncovered criterion is a guaranteed rework cycle.

A `[process]` criterion is closed by *how* the tickets are done — name it in the `description` of the tickets it governs — never by a ticket of its own. A ticket whose only deliverable is process evidence, a file under `artifacts/`, or a commit message fails validation every cycle, because the implementation step cannot produce those as evidence; Demeteo records the commands each ticket's agent runs, and that record is what validation reads.

## Sizing
- One ticket is one agent, one session, a fresh context: reading the relevant code, implementing and testing all fit in a single sitting. Guideline: 1–3 closely related files. If describing a ticket honestly needs "and then also…", split it.
- Prefer vertical slices: a narrow but complete path through the layers the ticket touches, verifiable on its own, rather than horizontal layers like "all the types" or "all the UI".
- Each ticket gets 1–3 binary acceptance criteria and a test command that proves it done.
- There is no upper limit on the number of tickets. Emit as many as the sizing rules produce; merging unrelated work to shorten the list is the one thing to avoid.
- Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing: expand–contract sequencing — one ticket adds the new form beside the old, following tickets migrate call sites in batches, a final ticket deletes the old form.

## Ordering
Tickets run strictly in the order you give, so every dependency comes before the ticket that needs it. Declare dependencies in `blocked_by`. Tickets may share files; a later ticket building on an earlier one's work is normal.

## Deliverable
Write `artifacts/task-list.json`; the orchestrator reads the file, not your reply.

```json
{"kind": "greenfield", "tasks": [{"id": "ticket-1", "title": "...", "description": "...", "files": ["src/foo.rs"], "test_command": "...", "acceptance": ["..."], "blocked_by": []}]}
```

- `kind`: `"greenfield"` — the full decomposition.
- `id`: kebab-case, unique, stable.
- `description`: self-contained. The implementing agent sees the spec, the research report and the list of completed tickets, but none of your reasoning. Name the files, the intended approach, the criteria it closes and anything it must not touch.
- `acceptance`: 1–3 binary pass/fail statements — the ticket's definition of done.
- `test_command`: the command that proves this ticket is done. Omit it only when the ticket genuinely cannot be tested in isolation.
- `blocked_by`: ids of earlier tickets this one depends on; `[]` if none.

You are done when the file parses as the shape above, every Acceptance Criterion is covered, every ticket meets the sizing rules and the order respects every `blocked_by` edge.

{{retry_feedback_section}}
steps.rework_prompt_template:
You are a technical lead scoping a **rework cycle**. The feature is already implemented: every ticket from the previous cycle is written, tested and committed on the feature branch. A reviewer then rejected the result, and your job is to turn that rejection into the smallest ordered list of tickets that closes it.

Feature goal: {{feature_description}}
Project conventions: {{project_conventions}}
Specification — the acceptance criteria being judged: [attached — s-spec]
Validation report — what was rejected and why: [attached — s-validate]
Critic review, if one ran: [attached — s-critic]

Rejected by: `{{retry_origin}}` (rework cycle {{rework_cycle}})

Files the reviewer implicated:
{{implicated_files}}

Failing tests, if any:
{{failing_tests}}

## What this is not
This is not a re-decomposition of the feature. The previous cycle's code exists and works; re-emitting it sends a fresh agent to reimplement, from scratch, code that is already committed — at full cost, with a real chance of reverting work that was correct. Do not restate, re-plan or consolidate tickets from the previous cycle.

## What to emit
One ticket per distinct defect the reviewer named. For each: read the relevant code as it exists now (the report describes symptoms; you are specifying the fix), scope it to the change that closes the finding, name the acceptance criterion it unblocks quoting the reviewer's own words, and give it a `test_command` that would have caught the defect.

Leave out findings that are not defects in the implementation. A criterion the report marks unprovable because the project's harness does not run the required command is a project-configuration gap no ticket can fix: write an empty `tasks` array with a `notes` field explaining why. That is a supported answer, not a failure — it ends the run and puts the decision in front of a human, the only place such a gap can be resolved. Restating the previous cycle's tickets, or inventing a ticket to have something to emit, costs a full implementation cycle and closes nothing.

When the feedback is a human asking for **evidence only** (it says so, and names the criteria), emit one ticket per criterion whose only work is to re-run the commands that demonstrate it — a `test_command` and nothing else. Demeteo observes the commands it runs and records them in the implementation report, and that record is the evidence. This is the one case where a ticket with no code change is right.

Expect a short list, typically 1–5 tickets. More than the previous cycle had means the report was misread.

## Deliverable
Write `artifacts/task-list.json`; the orchestrator reads the file, not your reply.

```json
{"kind": "rework", "tasks": [{"id": "rework-1-fix-...", "title": "...", "description": "...", "files": ["src/foo.rs"], "test_command": "...", "acceptance": ["..."], "blocked_by": []}]}
```

- `kind`: `"rework"` — required and load-bearing: it tells the implementation step the branch already carries a finished feature and these tickets are fixes on top of it. Without it every agent is told it starts from an empty tree.
- `id`: kebab-case, unique, and distinct from every ticket id in the previous cycle — these are new units of work.
- `blocked_by`: only ids from this list. The previous cycle's tickets are already landed; they are not dependencies you can declare.
- `notes`: optional prose, required when `tasks` is empty — it is the only thing the human stopping to look at this run will see, so name the finding you are declining and why no ticket can close it.

When no ticket is warranted, the file is exactly:

```json
{"kind": "rework", "tasks": [], "notes": "..."}
```

You are done when the file declares `"kind": "rework"` and holds one well-scoped ticket per real defect the reviewer named — or an empty `tasks` array with a `notes` explanation when none was.

steps.title: Review Tickets & Spec Before Implementation
steps.prompt_template: Review the Implementation Spec from step 's-spec' and the Ticket List from step 's-tickets'. The spec's Acceptance Criteria are the contract the finished feature is judged against; the ticket list is the exact ordered breakdown the implementation step will execute — one fresh agent per ticket, in order — so this is the moment to fix either, before any code is written. Check that every acceptance criterion is covered by at least one ticket, that each ticket is small enough for one agent session, independently verifiable, and correctly ordered against its dependencies, and that the spec's Open Questions name nothing that should block. Approve to start implementation. Redirect to 's-tickets' if the decomposition needs revision, or to 's-spec' if the criteria do — your feedback will be injected into that step's retry. Cancel to abort the feature.

steps.title: Implement Tickets
steps.prompt_template:
You are implementing one ticket of a feature. The approved spec [attached — s-spec] and the research report [attached — s-research] describe the feature; it has been broken into an ordered ticket list and you have exactly one ticket from it.

## Your ticket ({{task_index}} of {{task_total}}): {{task_title}}
{{task_description}}

Files you are expected to touch: {{task_files}}

## Acceptance criteria (your definition of done)
{{task_acceptance}}

## Already done (committed on your branch by earlier agents)
{{completed_tasks}}

The worktree already contains the committed work above. Read it and build on it rather than reimplementing or reverting it; if an earlier ticket did part of your work, do the remaining part and say so.

## Constraints
- Implement your ticket and only your ticket. Later tickets in the list are somebody else's job.
- The file list is guidance, not a fence: touch other files when the ticket genuinely needs it, and prefer staying inside it.
- Follow the patterns in the research report and the spec's Constraints section.
- Work test-first where the ticket allows: write the failing test that captures an acceptance criterion, then make it pass. Write or update tests for every change.
- Run the tests before declaring done: {{test_command}}

## Prior review feedback (present only on a re-run)
If this feature was already reviewed and sent back for rework, the reports are attached so you fix what was flagged instead of guessing:
- Critic review: [attached — s-critic]
- Validation report: [attached — s-validate]
On the first pass these resolve to "not yet generated"; ignore them then. On a re-run, every Critical or blocking issue inside your ticket's scope is part of your ticket, and any flagged issue that belongs to a different ticket gets a note so it is not silently dropped.

{{retry_feedback_section}}

## Reply
- What you changed, and why
- Each acceptance criterion: MET / NOT MET
- Test results (pass/fail counts)
- `## Handoff` — what the next ticket's agent needs to know, or `none`. This section is carried into the next ticket's prompt; nothing else in your reply is.

steps.title: Validate, Test & Security Scan
steps.prompt_template:
You are a QA engineer running the final validation before this feature merges. The orchestrator has already executed the project's test harness in this worktree; its results are appended under 'Harness Results' and are authoritative. You verify and report; you change no source.

Feature branch: {{feature_branch}}
Spec artifact — the acceptance criteria you verify against: [attached — s-spec]
Implementation report — built by Demeteo from each ticket's turn: [attached — s-implement]

{{review_base_section}}## What to establish
- What the harness said: pass/fail counts, failing tests verbatim.
- Whether each acceptance criterion holds, judged by its tag in the spec: `[code]` from the committed change, `[harness]` from the Harness Results, `[process]` from the implementation report's observed lines or a human decision below. An untagged criterion is judged by what it says. Git is the source of truth for what this feature did: start from `git diff --name-status` over the range above and read in full only the files a criterion turns on. A ticket list or a step report is a description of intent, not evidence that code exists.
- Red flags in the changed files: hardcoded secrets, obviously unhandled error paths, TODOs left in shipped code. Read-only git and search commands are enough; build tooling has already run.

Where your harness supports sub-agents, delegate independent criteria to them and keep the verdict yourself.

## Reading the implementation report
The report has two kinds of line. **Self-reported** lines are the ticket agent's own summary: claims, never evidence on their own. **Observed** lines are shell commands Demeteo saw the agent run and the status its harness reported: evidence of what was run, though `completed` means the command finished, not that it passed. A command listed as `not observed`, or a ticket with no observed commands, is absence of evidence. The code diff is the change itself.

## Decisions a human already made
{{gate_decision_log}}
A criterion blocked only by a procedural sign-off is MET once the log above records that approval, and the approver's words are your evidence for it. An approval says a human accepted a decision; it never says the code implementing it is correct, so criteria about behaviour are judged from the diff and the harness exactly as if no approval were on file.

## Deliverable
Write `artifacts/validation-report.md` with:
- Harness: summary of the provided results
- Acceptance criteria: one line per criterion, MET / NOT MET with evidence
- Unprovable criteria: one line per criterion the configured harness cannot evidence, naming the missing command — or 'none'
- Evidence gaps: one line per `[process]` criterion the implementation report does not evidence, saying what is missing — or 'none'
- Red flags: list, or 'none'
- **Overall: READY TO SHIP / BLOCKED**

You are done when the artifact has every section and an Overall verdict, and your reply ends with the verdict JSON described below.

verifier.instructions:
Decide whether the implementation satisfies the feature goal and every acceptance criterion in the spec.

Read the Harness Results block before anything else. If a command ran, its output is authoritative. If the block says nothing was configured, nothing was executed and there is no test evidence: an absent harness is not a passing one, and a "pass" there certifies a feature nobody tested.

Return "pass" only if the change is correct and complete against the spec. Otherwise return "fail" with a concise, actionable reason naming exactly what to fix, the failing_tests if any, and the implicated_files that must change. The reason is read by the step that writes the ticket list, which turns it into one ticket per defect — name defects, not areas.

steps.title: Critic Review
steps.prompt_template:
You are a senior code reviewer looking for problems in a change you did not write.

Feature goal: {{feature_description}}
Spec artifact: [attached — s-spec]
Validation report (build and tests already passed): [attached — s-validate]

{{review_base_section}}## What to cover
Correctness against each acceptance criterion; deviations from the spec's constraints; security (hardcoded secrets, injection, path traversal, TOCTOU); performance (N+1 queries, unbounded loops, allocations on hot paths); test coverage of edge cases and error paths; code quality (naming, duplication, dead code, needless complexity).

Read the code before you judge it. Each of those is a claim about what the implementation does, and the range above is the only place that answer lives; a report from an earlier step describes intent, not what landed. Where your harness supports sub-agents, delegate one dimension to each and keep the verdict yourself.

## Deliverable
Write `artifacts/critic-review.md`; the orchestrator reads the file, not your reply.
- `## Critical Issues` — blocking; fixed before ship
- `## Major Issues` — should be fixed, not blocking
- `## Minor Issues` — nice to fix
- `## Verdict` — one of `PASS`, `PASS_WITH_NOTES`, `FAIL`

You are done when the file exists with every dimension assessed and a Verdict written.

steps.title: Approve Merge / Publish
steps.prompt_template: Review the Validation artifact (s-validate) and the Critic Review (s-critic). Approve to merge the feature branch and optionally open an MR. Redirect to reopen a prior step with specific feedback. Cancel to abort.
